# Week 1 : Backend Architecture, Simulation Engine, and AWS Integration

The first week of the project focused on establishing the foundational architecture required for a real-time logistics simulation platform. We began by defining the overall system design, outlining a pipeline that connects a FastAPI backend simulation engine to an AWS DynamoDB database for persistent storage, and finally to a browser-based frontend powered by Leaflet.js and WebSockets. Once the architecture was set, we implemented the core backend simulation engine using FastAPI and asyncio. This included building the /start-sim endpoint to initialize trips, a WebSocket endpoint for streaming updates to the frontend, and helper modules for routing, geospatial calculations, and time estimation. The simulation logic for both trucks and ships was developed, since trucks follow realistic polyline paths obtained from the OSRM routing API, and ships follow stochastic movements near Basra Port to represent maritime activity.

A major achievement in Week 1 was integrating AWS DynamoDB as the persistent storage layer. We organized the database to store truck states, ship states, route polylines, cumulative distance calculations, and metadata such as ETAs. We implemented serialization/deserialization helpers using Python’s Decimal type to satisfy DynamoDB’s type system to handle all the errors. Complex logic by the help of LLMs was added to reset simulation state safely using paginated Scan and Delete operations. By the end of the week, the backend was capable of generating realistic simulations, storing data in the cloud, and maintaining consistent state across iterations. This helped lay the foundation for the rest of our project. 

# Week 2 : Frontend Development, Deployment, and System Stabilization

Week 2 transitioned into building and refining the user-facing portion of the project. Using Leaflet.js, we implemented an interactive geospatial map capable of rendering trucks, ships, and routes in real time. Custom icons, popups with metadata, route polylines, and dynamic camera fitting were added to create a polished and intuitive interface. The frontend was connected to the backend WebSocket stream, allowing truck and ship locations to update every second. We also added UI enhancements, such as updated status labels, ETAs, progress tracking, and depot markers.

In parallel, we focused on deployment and system reliability. The backend was containerized and deployed to Fly.io, requiring modifications to ensure that FastAPI listened on the correct port (0.0.0.0:8080) and that environment variables for AWS access were properly handled. We also deployed the frontend as a static Quarto website to cPanel, updating JavaScript paths and WebSocket URLs for production. During Week 2, significant debugging was performed to resolve issues such as WebSocket disconnections, CORS restrictions, stale cached JavaScript files, and DynamoDB item type inconsistencies. By the end of the week, the system was fully integrated end-to-end: the frontend map could start a simulation, the backend could generate and update real-time data, and the database accurately stored and streamed operational states.

# Week 3 : Machine Learning Integration, Evaluation, and Final Documentation

The third week focused on improving the simulation with machine learning and preparing the full analytical and technical documentation. We implemented both unsupervised and supervised learning components as per the project requirement. For unsupervised learning, we created a KMeans clustering model trained on simulated operational features such as planned speed and remaining distance. The model grouped trucks into clusters representing fast, slow, and anomalous behavior patterns. For supervised learning, we generated a labeled dataset and trained a logistic regression model to estimate delay probability based on key trip characteristics. Both models were exported as .pkl files and integrated into the backend pipeline, allowing real-time inference inside the simulation loop. The frontend was updated to display each truck’s cluster assignment and delay risk percentage, completing the ML-enhanced monitoring system.

Significant effort in Week 3 was also devoted to debugging ML deployment issues, including dependency mismatches involving NumPy and scikit-learn. Many of the models and fly.io could work on older versions of the libraries. After resolving these issues and rebuilding the deployment image, the system began successfully generating real-time ML predictions. The final portion of the week was spent writing the technical report sections: data collection, data cleaning, EDA, unsupervised learning, supervised learning, system design, and implementation details.
